title: Fill in the Blank: Array and Struct Syntax
prompt: Fill in the missing mnemonics, extend options, and offsets that reach array elements and struct fields in memory.

blanks.prompt: An array of .dword values starts at the label nums. Give the number of bytes between one element and the next, in decimal.
blanks.explanation: Element i sits at the base address plus i times the element size, and one .dword is 8 bytes wide. Scaling by the element size instead of by 1 is what makes an index land on an element boundary.
blanks.hint: How many bytes does one .dword take?

blanks.prompt: Store w22 into a .word array based at x19, scaling the 64-bit index held in x20 inside the brackets.
blanks.explanation: The register offset form can scale the index for you: lsl 2 multiplies x20 by 4, the size of one .word element. That saves a separate shift instruction before the store.

blanks.prompt: Store w22 into the same .word array, this time with the index held in the 32-bit register w20.
blanks.explanation: A 32-bit index needs an extend option before it can be added to a 64-bit base. sxtw 2 sign-extends w20 to 64 bits and then scales it by 4, so a negative index still computes the right address.

blanks.prompt: A date struct has field offsets date_year, date_month, and date_day. An employee struct holds a date at offset employee_start. With the employee record base in x19, store the day byte from w20.
blanks.explanation: Offsets into a nested struct add up: employee_start reaches the inner date, and date_day reaches the field inside it. The assembler evaluates the sum and encodes one constant offset.
blanks.hint: Add the offset of the field inside the nested struct.

blanks.prompt: The record base is in x19 and rec_b is the offset of a signed char field. Load that field into a 32-bit register.
blanks.explanation: ldrsb loads one byte and sign-extends it across all 32 bits of w21, so a stored -1 reads back as -1. ldrb would zero-extend the same byte to 255.
